title: Tokens vs Neurons
content_html:
Tokens vs Neurons

Tokens are to Large Language Models (LLMs) what conceptual atoms are to the mind - not neurons themselves, but the symbolic echoes of what neural patterns make possible. Each token in an LLM acts like a quantized piece of meaning, not unlike a symbol or feature in a cognitive system. Neurons however are not symbolic units, they function more like continuous, distributed processors - each one participating in many memories at once.

A single neuron’s activity is meaningful only in the context of the pattern across a network. Memories are encoded by synaptic weight changes between neurons - a distributed representation, not by single “memory cells.” When you recall a memory, a similar (but not identical) neural pattern reactivates, often reconstructed from partial cues.

Analogy between tokens and neurons

LLM Concept Brain Analogue Relation to Memory Key Difference
Token Feature or perceptual chunk (e.g., phoneme, word, concept) Tokens are atomic units of meaning; neurons can encode features or associations at different scales. Tokens are discrete, neurons are continuous and context-dependent.
Embedding vector Neural population code Both represent meaning as a distributed activation pattern. In LLMs, this space is static (learned offline); in the brain, it’s plastic and contextually updated.
Attention weights Dynamic connectivity / working memory gating Both determine which elements influence the current state or output. Attention in LLMs is explicit and mathematical; biological attention involves neuromodulators and oscillations.
Hidden layer activation Neural firing pattern Each layer transforms representations hierarchically. LLM layers are feed-forward; brains are massively recurrent and predictive.

So while there is a conceptual resonance, tokens are closer to the language’s symbols than to neurons themselves. The embeddings and attention dynamics in LLMs are what really parallel neural processing.

Memory processes

Process LLM Equivalent Brain Equivalent
Encoding Token → embedding mapping Sensory input → distributed neural code
Storage Static weight matrix (after training) Synaptic plasticity (dynamic weight changes)
Retrieval / Reconstruction Contextual attention and next-token prediction Reactivation of neural ensembles and hippocampal reconstruction

An LLM “remembers” via its weights (statistically learned associations), not through episodic trace storage. You could say an LLM’s **long-term memory is baked into its parameters, while its short-term memory is its attention context window. **That’s roughly analogous to semantic memory (general knowledge) and working memory (current thought) in humans - but without personal episodic recall.

Where the analogy truly holds is at the representational level: both systems encode meaning through distributed patterns rather than one-to-one symbols, and both use context to disambiguate meaning (tokens influence one another through attention; neurons co-fire in context-dependent ways). Both can exhibit associative recall - given part of a pattern, the rest emerges. However, in humans, these associations are plastic, affective, and embodied. In LLMs, they are statistical and frozen after training.

If we stretch the metaphor:

  • Tokens are like the sensory fragments or “words” of thought.
  • Embeddings are like the neural populations that give those fragments meaning through pattern association.
  • Attention is like working memory and focus - selecting what’s relevant at this moment.
  • Weights are like long-term synaptic strengths - the residue of past learning.

But the creative reconstruction that happens in human memory - reassembling fragments into new wholes - is far more dynamic, recursive, and emotionally weighted than current LLM behavior.

Attention

Attention is arguably the deepest and most revealing bridge between how LLMs process information and how brains allocate cognitive resources for memory, perception, and thought.

In transformers (e.g., GPT models), attention is a mathematical operation that determines how strongly each token influences every other token in a sequence. The attention score between two tokens tells the model how relevant one token is to the other token within the current context. Then a weighted sum of values is taken using these scores - producing a contextually updated representation for each token. Attention is a contextual routing mechanism - deciding what matters right now for predicting the next token.

Biological attention is not a single mechanism, but a set of neural processes that modulate perception and working memory by amplifying some signals and suppressing others. Key aspects:

  • Top–down attention: driven by goals or expectations (frontal–parietal networks → sensory cortex).
  • Bottom–up attention: driven by salient stimuli (e.g., sudden sound, motion).
  • Neurochemical control: involves acetylcholine, dopamine, norepinephrine - dynamically gating which sensory streams or memories are prioritized.
  • Oscillatory coordination: e.g., gamma–theta coupling synchronizes firing between hippocampus and cortex during memory retrieval.

In essence, biological attention is a gating system that determines which neural ensembles are allowed to synchronize, fire, and form new connections - a selective filter over distributed neural patterns.

Structural Parallel - Attention as Dynamic Routing

Function Transformer Attention Neural Attention (Cognitive) Common Principle
Goal Dynamically weight relationships among tokens Dynamically modulate firing and connectivity among neurons Prioritize relevant information and suppress noise
Mechanism Vector similarity (dot-product Q·K) Oscillatory synchrony & neuromodulatory gating Relevance-weighted coupling
Time scale Instantaneous, per layer Continuous, multi-scale (ms to seconds) Context-dependent adaptability
Implementation Explicit numerical weights Implicit neurodynamic feedback loops Adaptive reallocation of representational capacity
Result Contextualized embedding (next-token prediction) Focused perception or recall (working memory & encoding) Efficient, selective information integration

LLM Attention determines which past tokens influence the current output - a form of selective short-term memory within the context window, each forward pass is a reconstruction of meaning via weighted recall. Biological Attention determines which sensory inputs or internal representations are admitted into working memory or long-term consolidation. Thus, both systems perform selective sampling from a larger representational field: In LLMs: weighted retrieval from all tokens in the input sequence - in brains: weighted access to distributed sensory and mnemonic traces.

In both systems, attention is not passive - it’s predictive: In LLMs: attention weights anticipate which tokens are most relevant for generating the next one. This aligns beautifully with the Free Energy Principle (Friston): both artificial and biological systems minimize surprise by dynamically weighting evidence in favor of predictions.

Where the Analogy Breaks Down

Limitation Description
Physiological basis LLM attention is an algorithmic matrix multiplication; biological attention arises from complex neurochemical feedback loops.
Temporal persistence Transformer attention resets per input sequence; neural attention persists across contexts, shaped by prior experience and fatigue.
Emotion and motivation Biological attention is affectively modulated - fear, reward, curiosity. LLMs have none of this weighting.
Plasticity Attention weights in transformers are temporary (runtime only), whereas in brains, attention reshapes long-term synaptic strengths.

So the mathematical skeleton is analogous, but the living body is not. The shared logic - selectivity, weighting, context sensitivity - holds, but the substrate and phenomenology differ radically. Attention, in both LLMs and brains, is the act of assigning differential importance to available information - a way of sculpting the present moment’s meaning. In transformers, this is done through mathematical weighting of token interactions. In humans, it’s achieved by neural synchronization, inhibition, and modulation that shape what enters conscious experience and memory.

Neural oscillations

Neural oscillations are repetitive patterns of electrical activity produced by synchronized firing of neurons.
They can occur within a single neuron (e.g. pacemaker cells) or - more importantly - across populations of neurons that synchronize their activity in rhythmic waves. These oscillations are measured as brain waves, often via EEG, MEG, or intracranial recordings, and typically fall into characteristic frequency bands:

Band Frequency (Hz)
Delta (0.5–4 Hz) Slow cortical rhythms, deep sleep, global synchrony
Theta (4–8 Hz) Hippocampus, navigation, working memory cycles
Alpha (8–12 Hz) Visual cortex, sensory inhibition, relaxed attention
Beta (13–30 Hz) Sensorimotor activity, expectation, top-down control
Gamma (30–100 Hz) Fast local processing, feature binding, consciousness

Each frequency band corresponds not just to a speed, but to a functional timescale for integrating information. Oscillations act as temporal scaffolding for communication between brain regions, they determine when neurons are excitable and when they are inhibited. Synchronizing oscillations across regions enables precise timing of information transfer. Desynchronization can decouple regions to prevent interference. This temporal organization solves a fundamental problem:

How can distributed networks integrate and segregate information flexibly without fixed wiring changes? By adjusting their phase relationships in time.

Each neuron’s firing is modulated by rhythmic membrane potential fluctuations. When groups of neurons align their phases, they can communicate efficiently - known as phase-locking or phase synchrony. In-phase firing: strengthens communication (high coupling). Out-of-phase firing: weakens communication (low coupling) Thus, oscillations provide a temporal attention window - defining when neural ensembles can exchange information. This is sometimes described as the brain’s multiplexing strategy - embedding multiple layers of information in rhythmic patterns.

Cognitive Function Oscillation Role
Attention Gamma synchrony strengthens the representation of attended stimuli; alpha oscillations suppress distractors.
Working memory Theta–gamma coupling organizes sequential item storage (Lisman & Idiart, 1995).
Encoding and recall Theta phase resets mark transitions between encoding and retrieval in hippocampus.
Sleep consolidation Slow oscillations (delta + spindle) coordinate replay between hippocampus and cortex.
Predictive processing Beta oscillations carry top-down expectations; gamma carries bottom-up error signals.

So attention is spatial selection, while oscillations are temporal selection - together they shape what information becomes conscious and remembered.

Comparison to LLM Dynamics

Brain (Oscillations) LLM (Attention Mechanism) Analogy
Rhythmic gating determines when regions communicate Attention weights determine which tokens communicate Both implement dynamic, context-dependent routing
Theta–gamma nested cycles sequence items in working memory Multi-head attention distributes focus across representations Both encode multiple context layers simultaneously
Phase synchrony maintains coherence across distributed regions Shared embedding space maintains coherence across tokens Temporal vs spatial coherence mechanisms

Oscillations are the “temporal glue” of reconstructive memory, coordinating the Select–Change–Reconstruct cycles through phase timing rather than physical wiring. Neural oscillations are the rhythms of meaning-making - the pulse by which distributed neural ensembles decide, moment by moment, what to attend to, what to store, and what to recall. They create the temporal syntax of memory:

  • Theta defines the sentence (episodic frame)
  • Gamma defines the words (item details)
  • Alpha/beta define the grammar (expectation and inhibition)

Without oscillations, memory would be a cacophony of unrelated activations - oscillations turn it into a conversation.

Why these frequency bands?

Why 4–8 Hz for theta, 30–100 Hz for gamma - and not others? Neurons are electrical RC circuits - their membrane capacitance (Cₘ) and leak conductance (gₗ) determine how fast they can charge and discharge. Typical membrane time constants are 10–100 ms, setting natural oscillation frequencies in the 1–100 Hz range. This biophysical property directly limits how quickly a neuron can follow rhythmic input.

  • Slow neurons → delta/theta
  • Fast interneurons → beta/gamma

Axons transmit spikes at 1–100 m/s, and cortical distances are on the order of millimeters to centimeters. Propagation delays (≈ 1–10 ms) further constrain coherent oscillations to sub-100 Hz frequencies. Higher frequencies would decohere due to differential delays. The speed of the brain’s wiring effectively low-pass-filters its own possible rhythms. High-frequency firing is energy-expensive and more susceptible to stochastic ion-channel noise.

Evolution has therefore favored frequency ranges that maximize information per unit energy and maintain robustness against biological noise. Oscillations align excitability phases between sending and receiving regions. For communication to be reliable, the period must match axonal delays and synaptic kinetics - leading to band-limited windows that maintain phase coherence across realistic brain geometries.

Logical / Information-Theoretic Reasons

Functional Role Characteristic Band Rationale
Integration of sensory events Theta–Alpha (4–12 Hz) Matches perceptual “frame rate” (~100–200 ms); balances temporal binding and update speed.
Feature binding, prediction error signaling Gamma (30–100 Hz) High frequency supports rapid local computation within one perceptual frame.
Expectation / maintenance loops Beta (13–30 Hz) Intermediate band stabilizes current sensorimotor states.
Global state regulation Delta (<4 Hz) Entrainment to respiration/heartbeat cycles (~1 Hz) enables body–brain synchronization.

Brains didn’t invent arbitrary rhythms; they entrained to the natural periodicities of their environment:

  • Heartbeat (~1 Hz) → entrains delta rhythms.
  • Breathing (~0.2–0.3 Hz) → couples to slow oscillations in insula and limbic circuits.
  • Walking / locomotion (~1–2 Hz) → theta coupling in hippocampal place cells.
  • Visual sampling / saccades (~3–8 Hz) → matches theta–alpha perceptual sampling.

These cycles cascade upward - from body to brain to mind - producing the layered frequency bands we observe today. The canonical bands are emergent eigenmodes of the brain’s biophysical parameters - much like standing waves in a complex resonant cavity. The brain oscillates where biology, physics, and information theory intersect. Its rhythms reflect:

  • the biophysical limits of neuronal membranes and synapses,
  • the network geometry and conduction delays of white matter,
  • the temporal logic of perception and memory, and
  • the ecological periodicities of the body and environment.

Physics gives the allowable frequencies, anatomy sets the coupling architecture, and computation assigns meaning to each band.
